_source: Transcribed from the GWMS Curriculum Guide in Notion. Per-session fields come from that session's Lesson and Intervention Guide (Unit 7). Card, domain and keyCondition come from the GWMS Technical Map. Where the two name the game differently, the Lesson and Intervention Guide wins, because it is the per-session authority.

stage.name: The Initiation
stage.grapplingTlo: By the end of the Initiation, participants will apply chest-pin control and its owned finishes to make contact, hold it under resistance, and reset cleanly after a break, releasing on every tap.
stage.caselTlo: By the end of the Initiation, participants will apply social awareness and relationship skills to make real contact with others, tolerate friction, own their part in a rupture, and attempt repair.
stage.connection: Chest-to-chest contact on the mat is like contact with people. Friction on the mat is like friction with people. A break on the mat is like a rupture between people. A reset on the mat is like repair between people. The Initiation tests the real you against other people.

wrongAnswers.text: Holding the finish after your partner taps
wrongAnswers.feedback: Never. Let go the instant your partner taps. Every single time. The tap is law.
You keep the pin by feeling your partner and moving with them, not by clamping down and squeezing hard. Staying calm beats forcing harder.

sessions.probingQuestion: What happens in you when someone makes real contact?
sessions.keyCondition: Chest on chest with hips and shoulders covered, three-count.
sessions.gameName: Chest to Chest Under Elbows Maintenance
sessions.gameText: The top player holds chest to chest, under both elbows. Win by keeping that contact for a three-count while the bottom player moves.
sessions.gameNote: This is the most direct contact there is, chest to chest, face to face. Making it and holding it is like letting someone get close to you.
sessions.gameWin: Keeping chest-on-chest contact under both elbows for a three-count
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will make and hold chest-to-chest contact with a partner who is pushing back a little.
grapplingElos: Get into a chest-pin position and hold it for a three-count against light resistance.
Keep safe, steady contact with a partner during rolling. Don't let go.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what they feel when someone makes real contact with them, and say how that connects to meeting people in real life.
caselElos: Notice one feeling in their body or mind during close contact.
Connect that feeling to how they meet people outside the room.
sessions.connection: Holding contact on the mat and noticing what contact does to you are the same skill. Both mean staying present when someone gets close, instead of pushing them away. The pin teaches your body to stay. Thinking about it teaches your mind why staying is hard.
sessions.takeaway: Contact does something to all of us. Now you can feel yours.

sessions.probingQuestion: How much of someone else do you actually let in?
sessions.keyCondition: Keep the coverage as the partner moves.
sessions.gameText: The top player keeps control of the partner's elbows as the partner pushes and tries to make space. Win by keeping the elbows controlled the whole time.
sessions.gameNote: You keep the pin by feeling your partner and adjusting, not by clamping down and squeezing. That's a lot like how much you actually let someone in.
sessions.gameWin: Keeping the elbows controlled the whole time as the partner pushes and moves
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will keep chest-pin control while reading and adjusting to a partner's movement, even as the partner tries to make space.
grapplingElos: Keep chest-pin control for a three-count while the partner pushes and moves.
Adjust pressure and connection to match the partner, instead of holding one hard grip.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will say how much they open up to another person, and name one thing that makes letting someone in hard.
caselElos: Notice if they feel closed off or open during close contact.
Name one thing that makes it hard to let another person in.
sessions.connection: Keeping a pin means feeling your partner and adjusting to them, not clamping down and ignoring them. Letting someone in works the same way. You hold the connection by reading the other person, not by shutting them out and pushing through alone.
sessions.takeaway: Letting people in is like a dial you control. You just found yours.

sessions.probingQuestion: Who are you with other people, now that you've met yourself?
sessions.keyCondition: Keep chest contact going the whole time.
sessions.gameText: From the top, stay under both elbows and keep the connection going as the partner works. There is no finish here, just holding real contact.
sessions.gameNote: Roll as the real you, not a performance. That is who you are with other people now.
sessions.gameWin: Staying under both elbows and keeping the connection alive the whole time
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will get into chest-pin control from a neutral start and keep it, rolling as their real self instead of putting on a show.
grapplingElos: Get into a chest pin from a neutral position and hold it.
Keep control without giving up the position when it gets hard.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will describe who they are with other people, now that the Descent named their real self.
caselElos: Name one way the real self shows up with others differently than the old mask did.
Connect that to how they want to be in their relationships.
sessions.connection: The Descent found the real you. Now it goes to the mat with a partner. Rolling as the real you, instead of a mask, is the same as showing up honest in a relationship instead of performing one.
sessions.takeaway: The real you is in the room now, and other people are in it too.

sessions.probingQuestion: What do you do when someone pushes back?
sessions.keyCondition: Hold the pin while the partner fights back hard, running 4S.
sessions.gameName: Mounted and Side Control Pin Game
sessions.gameText: The top player holds the pin while the partner works hard to escape. Win by covering the hips, staying under the elbow, and keeping hands connected, all at once, against real resistance.
sessions.gameNote: Pushback is the test. Staying calm and adjusting beats forcing harder.
sessions.gameWin: Hip coverage, under the elbow, and hands connected all at once, against real resistance
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will keep chest-pin control while a partner fights back hard.
grapplingElos: Keep the pin for a three-count while the partner fights back and tries to escape.
Respond to resistance by staying balanced and adjusting, not by panicking or using raw force.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what they do when another person pushes back, and say if that habit helps them or hurts them.
caselElos: Name their usual response to pushback.
Say whether that response helps or hurts the relationship.
sessions.connection: A partner resisting the pin is pushback made physical. What you do when they fight the pin is usually what you do when people push back in life. Both reward staying calm and adjusting over forcing harder.
sessions.takeaway: Pushback is normal. Your response to it is a choice, not a reflex you're stuck with.

sessions.probingQuestion: Can you stay present when it gets uncomfortable?
sessions.keyCondition: Trap one arm and keep it trapped while the partner tries to get it back.
sessions.gameText: The top player traps and pins a wrist while the partner tries to break free. Win by keeping the wrist trapped and reaching head-and-arm or chest-to-back contact.
sessions.gameNote: You are staying in an uncomfortable spot and working it instead of bailing out.
sessions.gameWin: Keeping the wrist trapped and reaching head-and-arm or chest-to-back contact
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will stay in a hard chest-pin exchange, even when it feels uncomfortable, instead of bailing out.
grapplingElos: Stay in a hard chest-pin position, even while the partner frames and bridges, for a set time without letting go.
Use a calming tool, like a breath or a base reset, to stay present under pressure.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will practice staying present when things feel uncomfortable, and name what makes them want to bail.
caselElos: Notice the moment they usually want to leave a hard conversation or situation.
Practice one way to stay present instead of leaving.
sessions.connection: Staying in an uncomfortable pin instead of scrambling out is like staying in a hard conversation. Both take the same skill: putting up with discomfort instead of running from it.
sessions.note: Staying is the skill. But leaving a harmful situation is wise, not a failure.
sessions.takeaway: You can stay when things feel uncomfortable. You just did it.

sessions.probingQuestion: What does your friction do to the people across from you?
sessions.keyCondition: Firm control that keeps the partner safe. Adjust the moment they tap.
sessions.gameName: Hip Control Breakdown Game, run with an intensity constraint
sessions.gameText: The top player breaks the partner down and takes control, hips down, shoulder connected, with a limit on how hard they go. Win by holding control while keeping the partner completely safe.
sessions.gameNote: You can pin hard and still not hurt them. That choice is yours, every round.
sessions.gameWin: Holding control — hips down, shoulder connected — while keeping the partner completely safe
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will use chest-pin control hard enough to work, but controlled enough to keep the partner safe.
grapplingElos: Apply the pin firmly while keeping the partner safe.
Adjust how hard they go based on the partner's signals and taps.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name how their conflict style affects other people, and one change they can make.
caselElos: Notice how their friction lands on the person across from them.
Name one change that keeps the friction honest but not harmful.
sessions.connection: You can pin someone hard and still keep them safe. That is control of your own force. Your conflict off the mat lands on real people too, and the same control applies: honest friction, not harm.
sessions.takeaway: Friction is fine. Harm is a choice. The control is yours.

sessions.probingQuestion: What breaks in you when a connection breaks?
sessions.keyCondition: Frame first, then bridge. Reset clean after the break.
sessions.gameText: This one is from the bottom. The pin breaks and you get reversed or stuck underneath. Win by framing first, then standing and turning to face your partner.
sessions.gameNote: Reset clean, no payback. That is how you handle a break when a connection goes bad.
sessions.gameWin: Framing first, then standing and turning to face — a clean reset
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will notice when chest-pin control breaks, and reset to a safe position without panic or payback.
grapplingElos: Notice the moment control is lost, a reversal or an escape.
Reset to a safe position instead of forcing it or trying to get payback.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what breaks inside them when a connection breaks.
caselElos: Notice how they react inside when a relationship or connection breaks.
Name whether they tend to strike back, shut down, or pull away.
sessions.connection: Losing the pin and getting reversed is a small rupture. How you handle that break on the mat, a clean reset or payback, is a lot like how you handle broken connections in life.
sessions.takeaway: A rupture teaches you something. You survived naming it.

sessions.probingQuestion: Have you ever broken something with someone and left it broken?
sessions.keyCondition: Trap the choking-side arm before the frame closes. Release the instant your partner taps.
sessions.gameName: Mount Head and Arm Trap Game
sessions.gameText: This is the first finish you own: a strangle. Trap the head and one arm, hands locked together. Trap the choking-side arm before the frame closes. Release the instant your partner taps. Every single time.
sessions.gameNote: This is power you can use and then let go of. The tap is an invitation to repair. This week asks if you take it.
sessions.gameWin: Trapping the head and one arm with hands locked — and releasing the instant your partner taps
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will apply one owned chest-pin finish, a strangle, with full control, and release the instant their partner taps.
grapplingElos: Get one owned chest-pin finish locked in against light resistance.
Release instantly and completely on the partner's tap, every time.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name a rupture they left unrepaired, without having to share it out loud.
caselElos: Admit there's a broken connection they never fixed.
Notice what leaving it broken has cost them.
sessions.connection: A finish you can apply and release on the tap is power you control. Leaving a break unrepaired is choosing not to release, not to reset. The tap is the invitation to repair. This week asks whether you take it.
sessions.takeaway: Naming the break you never fixed is the first step toward repair.

sessions.probingQuestion: When something breaks, what part is yours to own?
sessions.keyCondition: Both hands controlling the wrist, set before you straighten the arm. Release the instant your partner taps.
sessions.gameText: This is the second finish you own: an arm lock. Separate your partner's hands and get two grips on the wrist. Set both control points before you straighten the arm. Release the instant they tap.
sessions.gameNote: Owning your part when something breaks starts with control, not a yank.
sessions.gameWin: Separating the hands and getting two grips on the wrist, with control set before straightening the arm
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will apply a second owned chest-pin finish, an arm lock, with control, and name one mistake they made in a round without making excuses.
grapplingElos: Get an owned chest-pin arm lock locked in with control, and release on the tap.
Name one mistake they made in a round honestly, without blaming the partner.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will say which part of a break is their share, separate from the other person's share.
caselElos: Tell apart their share of a rupture from the other person's share.
Name the one piece of it that belongs to them.
sessions.connection: On the mat you can name your own mistake in a round without blaming your partner. Owning your part of a rupture works the same way. It starts with separating your piece from theirs.
sessions.takeaway: Owning your part is the doorway to repair.

sessions.probingQuestion: What does it take for you to say sorry and mean it?
sessions.keyCondition: Get back in and rebuild the pin after a scramble.
sessions.gameText: After a scramble, rebuild the pin cleanly. Win by covering the hips, getting under the elbow, and connecting your hands again.
sessions.gameNote: Slap hands and roll clean after a hard round. That reset is repair in the body.
sessions.gameWin: Covering the hips, getting under the elbow, and connecting your hands again after a scramble
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will reset with a partner after a hard round and rebuild chest-pin control cleanly.
grapplingElos: Get back in and rebuild a chest pin after a scramble or reversal.
Roll with a partner right after a heated round, without carrying a grudge into it.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what it takes for them to give a real apology.
caselElos: Name what a real apology takes from them.
Tell apart a real apology from a dodge.
sessions.connection: Resetting and rolling clean with someone right after a hard round is like squaring up with words. A real apology is the same kind of reset: you get back in instead of carrying the grudge.
sessions.takeaway: Real repair has parts, and now you can name them.

sessions.probingQuestion: Can you stay when leaving would be easier?
sessions.keyCondition: Finish a hard round without giving up, in both roles.
sessions.gameName: Guard Recovery with Passing Resistance Game
sessions.gameText: Roll live, both roles, against a tough partner. On top, win by locking hands and holding the pin against real resistance.
sessions.gameNote: Stay in the hard round and keep working instead of asking to switch. Staying is a choice you make on purpose.
sessions.gameWin: On top, locking hands and holding the pin against real resistance
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will stay with a hard training partner and keep working instead of asking to switch.
grapplingElos: Finish a hard round with a tough partner without giving up or asking to switch.
Keep control and stay calm when the partnership is frustrating.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what makes them want to leave a hard relationship and one reason to stay.
caselElos: Notice their own urge to leave a hard relationship.
Name one thing worth staying for.
sessions.connection: Staying with a hard partner on the mat instead of switching is commitment made physical. Staying in a hard relationship when leaving is easier is the same choice. Both build the muscle of not bailing on people.
sessions.note: Staying is the skill. But leaving a harmful relationship is not failure. This is never an all-or-nothing rule.
sessions.takeaway: Staying is a choice you can make on purpose. You just practiced it.

sessions.probingQuestion: What does repair cost you, and is it worth paying?
sessions.keyCondition: Move between control and the owned finishes. Always honor the tap.
sessions.gameName: Hunt for Hips and Shoulders (Perpendicular Start)
sessions.gameText: Open rolling from the chest pin, both sides play. Move between control and the owned finishes. Honor the tap, reset, and keep going.
sessions.gameNote: This is the whole Initiation in one round: contact, friction, a break, and repair.
sessions.gameWin: Flowing between control and the owned finishes with the tap honored, resetting and continuing
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will put together chest-pin control and the finishes in open rolling, using everything they have learned so far.
grapplingElos: Move between chest-pin control and the owned finishes during live rolling.
Give and honor the tap, then reset and keep going cleanly.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what repair costs them, and decide if it's worth paying that cost.
caselElos: Name the personal cost of repairing a rupture, like pride, comfort, or time.
Decide whether repair is worth that cost, and say why.
sessions.connection: Open rolling puts it all together: control, finish, tap, reset, in one flow. Repair works the same way in relationships. It costs pride and comfort, and you decide it's worth paying. This closes the Initiation and points to the Return.
sessions.takeaway: You made contact, took the friction, survived the rupture, and learned repair.
